items.label: census and sample
items.hint: A census is exact but slow and costly; a sample estimates. An experiment changes something on purpose; an observation watches.

items.label: bias
items.hint: Bias pushes a result one way: sampling bias (who is asked), response bias (how they are asked), measurement bias (the tool). A bigger sample doesn't fix it.

widget: sample

items.shows: A convenience sample: all from Year 7, pushed high

items.label: sampling methods
items.hint: Simple random: same chance for all. Systematic: every kth from a random start. Stratified: at random within each group, in proportion. Convenience and quota: someone chooses, so they can be biased.

items.label: describing a sample
items.hint: Describe the shape (symmetric or skewed), the centre (mean, median) and the spread (range), then estimate the population with the method and size. Primary data you collect; secondary data others collected.

items.label: sampling variation
items.hint: Fair samples from one population give different results by chance. Their results scatter around the population's value, closer for bigger samples.

items.label: inference
items.code: \text{about } \ldots \text{, from a random sample of } n
items.hint: Infer only about the population sampled, give an estimate, and say how sure you are (size and method). Collect data with consent and anonymity.
